title: Living with aplastic anaemia | NHS inform
text:
Living with aplastic anaemia
Being diagnosed with aplastic anaemia can affect many different parts of your life. It can also affect those close to you.
Find out more about aplastic anaemia
Meet Barbara
In this video, Barbara talks about her experience with aplastic anaemia.
Day-to-day life
Aplastic anaemia can affect things in your day-to-day life. For example, it may mean you need to miss work or university, or ask for adjustments. You may also need to pause certain hobbies or activities.
If you have aplastic anaemia and a low white blood count, you’re at a higher risk of severe infections. This means you should get medical help quickly if you become unwell. You may also need to take more precautions to reduce your risk of getting inflections like a cold or flu. For example, you may need to avoid large gatherings and people who have minor illnesses.
Sometimes you may need to rely on others to help with things, like shopping or getting to hospital appointments.
The Aplastic Anaemia Trust has further advice on
living with aplastic anaemia
. This includes
emotional and wellbeing support
, and information on
how to deal with fatigue.
Living with fatigue
Fatigue is an overwhelming feeling of total exhaustion. Unlike tiredness, it doesn’t get better with rest and sleep.
Fatigue can mean that exercise or activities, including household chores like cleaning, can make you feel exhausted afterwards. Sometimes this feeling can last a couple of days.
Fatigue can also cause some uncertainty as you can’t always tell what each day will be like.
For many people with aplastic anaemia, it can be challenging to manage fatigue. It may help to:
build up what you do gradually
listen to your body
adjust how you do things – for example, move more slowly or perform tasks sitting down
try and avoid doing too much, even if there are periods when you feel more energetic
try not to feel pressurised to do things
Talk to your healthcare team if you need further support managing fatigue.
How to connect with other people
Aplastic anaemia is so rare that you may not have the opportunity to meet others with the condition. However, the
Aplastic Anaemia Trust
can help you connect with people who have experience of the condition, as well as parents of current and former aplastic anaemia patients.
The Aplastic Anaemia Trust offers services including:
a
support line
– whether you’ve been diagnosed with aplastic anaemia or just have questions about it, you can use the support line to talk to someone
events online or in person
– there are various events across Scotland and the UK where you can meet other people affected by aplastic anaemia
Patient Support Facebook Group
– if you have a Facebook account, people with aplastic anaemia and their families can join this group to connect with people who have experience of the condition
Mental health and wellbeing
There can be a lot of uncertainty and stress when you or someone close to you is diagnosed with aplastic anaemia. Sometimes it can take a while to get a diagnosis, which may add to these feelings.
It may help to:
talk to others about how you’re feeling
try relaxation techniques like meditation
do breathing and relaxation exercises
get advice if you’re struggling with stress
work through a self-help guide
to support your mental health and wellbeing
The Aplastic Anaemia Trust also provides
emotional wellbeing support
. You can be referred for 1-to-1 support sessions through the organisation.
Financial support
People affected by aplastic anaemia may be able to get some financial support.
In Scotland, the
Adult Disability Payment
can help if you have a disability or long-term health condition that affects your everyday life. For example, it can help with the cost of things like:
getting a taxi if you can’t walk
ordering food if you can’t cook
paying for a cleaner
Citizens Advice Scotland
have information on benefits. You can also contact your local
Citizens Advice Bureau
if you’d like further advice.
Social Security Scotland
also has information on the benefits they offer.
The Aplastic Anaemia Trust helpline
can help if you’re having trouble getting financial support or if you need further information on benefits. If needed, they can also refer you to financial support elsewhere.
Maggie’s
also have advice on benefits. You can speak to a Maggie’s Benefits Advisor to help find out what support applies to you. They can also help you fill out application forms.
Further information and support
The
Aplastic Anaemia Trust
has lots of information and support for people with aplastic anaemia, and those close to them.
The charity
Maggie’s
can support people living with aplastic anaemia and their families.
Marrowkidz
also provides information and advice for children and young people affected by aplastic anaemia.
If you have a genetic condition that causes aplastic anaemia, there are organisations that can support you. This includes:
Fanconi Hope
– information and support with Fanconi Anaemia
DC Action
– information and support with Dyskeratosis Congenita
SDS UK
– information and support with Shwachman Diamond Syndrome
The
PNH National Service
also provides information on Paroxysmal Nocturnal Haemoglobinuria (PNH).

The Aplastic Anaemia Trust
